n: Does vitamin C help iron absorption?
a: Yes, vitamin C increases the absorption of iron from plant foods and supplements. A glass of orange juice or a pepper with the meal is enough. Recent studies show the extra benefit with iron supplements is small.

n: Do I need vitamin D in winter?
a: From November to March the sun in Greece makes little vitamin D, and many people have low levels. People who stay indoors a lot, older adults and people with dark skin benefit from 800–1000 IU a day in winter.

n: How much vitamin D is too much?
a: The safe upper limit for adults is 4000 IU a day. Toxicity (high calcium, nausea, kidney stones) usually appears with tens of thousands of IU for months or with dosing mistakes. 25(OH)D levels above 100 ng/ml are very high.

MK-7 stays longer in the blood and is taken once a day (90–200 µg). MK-4 needs much larger doses. The data on bones and blood vessels are still limited for both. People on warfarin should not take K2 without their doctor.

n: Do B vitamins give you energy?
a: B vitamins are needed to produce energy, but they only give you energy if you are deficient. In people without a deficiency they do not fix tiredness. Fatigue needs checking for iron, B12, thyroid and sleep.

n: How long can I take zinc?
a: Up to 25–40 mg a day is safe. Higher doses for months cause copper deficiency, with anaemia and nerve damage. For long-term use above 25 mg, choose a product with 1–2 mg of copper.
It may raise thyroid hormones. Cases of hyperthyroidism have been reported. People with a thyroid condition or on thyroxine should ask their doctor and check their TSH.
The studies are few and small, mostly in older adults. The benefit is small: falling asleep a few minutes faster. It probably helps most in people who are deficient. It is safe to try.
Small studies show a small reduction in pain in osteoarthritis and in athletes, but they are often industry-funded. Strengthening exercises and weight loss help much more.

Yes. Creatine helps strength and muscle in women too, and it is being studied for bones after menopause. It can raise weight slightly because of water in the muscles, not fat. There is not enough data in pregnancy.
Small studies show a small improvement in memory, mainly in vegetarians, older adults and during sleep deprivation. The data are still early.
The body makes its own Q10. It is studied in heart failure, migraine and muscle pain from statins, with small or conflicting benefits. Healthy people do not need it.
Yes, at high doses. Meta-analyses show that more than 1 g a day increases the risk of atrial fibrillation by about 25%. People with an arrhythmia should ask their cardiologist.

Fish is better: besides omega-3 it has protein, vitamin D, selenium and iodine, and it is linked with fewer heart attacks. Capsules are an option for people who do not eat fish. Two portions of oily fish a week are enough.

n: Should I take a probiotic every day?
a: Healthy people do not need one. Probiotics have evidence for specific cases, such as diarrhoea from antibiotics and some irritable bowel symptoms. Fibre and fermented foods support the microbiome every day.
They are absorbed normally, but they often contain sugar, lower doses and lose potency over time. They look like sweets, so keep them away from children: iron overdose is dangerous.
Small studies show slightly better absorption for some (e.g. vitamin C, glutathione), but no proof of better health outcomes. They cost much more.

Regular drinking mainly lowers thiamine (B1), folate, B6, magnesium and zinc. B1 deficiency can seriously damage the brain. The answer is to cut down on alcohol, and in dependence to take B1 on medical advice.

n: How do I get enough iron as a vegan?
a: Legumes, tofu, seeds, nuts and green vegetables, with vitamin C in the same meal. Soaking and sprouting help. Keep tea and coffee away from meals. Check your ferritin once a year.

n: Do calcium supplements harm the heart?
a: Some meta-analyses found a small rise in heart attacks with supplements taken without vitamin D, others did not. Calcium from food does not raise the risk. It is better to get calcium from your diet and supplement only what is missing.

n: Why is vitamin A dangerous in pregnancy?
a: High doses of retinol (more than 10,000 IU a day) cause birth defects. Avoid supplements with retinol, liver and cod liver oil. Beta-carotene from fruit and vegetables is safe.

n: Which fish are safe in pregnancy?
a: 2–3 portions a week of low-mercury fish are recommended: sardines, anchovies, salmon, cod, sea bream. Avoid swordfish, shark and large tuna. Raw fish and seafood are best avoided.

n: How much coffee can I drink in pregnancy?
a: Up to 200 mg of caffeine a day, about 1–2 cups of filter coffee or 2 espressos. Tea, cola, chocolate and energy drinks count too.
Yes. Breastfed babies need 400 IU a day from the first days until their first birthday. Formula milks already contain vitamin D. Ask your paediatrician about the dose.
Children who eat fish 1–2 times a week do not need a supplement. In ADHD the benefit is small. If your child does not eat fish, a children's product is a reasonable choice.

n: When does a child need iron?
a: Only when tests show a deficiency. At risk are premature babies, babies who drink a lot of cow's milk before age 1, and teenage girls with heavy periods. Iron overdose is one of the most dangerous poisonings in children.

n: How much protein do I need after 65?
a: More than younger people: 1–1.2 g per kilo of body weight a day, spread over 3 meals with 25–30 g each. Together with strength exercises it prevents muscle loss. With kidney disease, only with your doctor.

n: Can I catch up on sleep at the weekend?
a: Partly. Extra sleep helps with tiredness, but it does not fully fix the metabolic effects of sleep loss. Big changes in wake-up time disrupt the body clock. A steady schedule is better.

n: Does walking after a meal help?
a: Yes. 10–15 minutes of walking after a meal reduces the rise in blood sugar, especially in diabetes. Even 2–5 minutes help.

n: How often should I do weight training?
a: Twice a week for all the major muscle groups is the WHO recommendation. Even 30–60 minutes a week is linked with lower mortality. Start light and increase gradually.

n: How fast is it safe to lose weight?
a: About 0.5–1 kg a week. Very fast loss increases muscle loss and the risk of gallstones. Very low-calorie diets only with medical supervision.

n: Do I lose muscle on the new weight loss medicines?
a: Part of the weight lost (about 25–40%) is lean mass, as with any large weight loss. Enough protein and strength exercises help keep the muscle.

n: Does eating late at night make you fat?
a: Total calories matter more. But studies show late meals raise blood sugar more and disturb sleep. It is good to have the last meal 2–3 hours before bed.
Studies do not show that seed oils harm the heart. When they replace saturated fat they lower cholesterol. They are not suited to repeated frying at high temperatures. Olive oil is the best choice.

For those who tolerate it, milk and especially yogurt are good sources of protein, calcium and iodine. It is not essential: calcium can come from other foods too. With lactose intolerance, yogurt and hard cheeses are usually tolerated.
No. It is also almost entirely sodium chloride. Its trace minerals are in very small amounts. It usually has no iodine, while iodised salt helps the thyroid.
Only slightly. Honey has some antioxidants, but for the body it is mostly sugar and it raises blood sugar. Use it in moderation. Never for babies under 1 year.
Chocolate with 70% cocoa or more has flavanols that lower blood pressure slightly. But it has many calories: 20–30 g a day is enough. Some products contain cadmium and lead.
Yes, it has good evidence for nausea in pregnancy and after surgery, less for travel sickness. Usually 1 g a day in divided doses. In pregnancy ask your doctor.

Ferritin rises with inflammation, fatty liver, alcohol, obesity and iron overload (e.g. haemochromatosis, transfusions). Transferrin saturation also needs measuring. Stop any iron supplement until you are checked.
